articles.title: California rejected Billionaire tax with 53 to 47 percent 'no' vote, 'lot thanks' to Sergey Brin; but 5 other states are preparing bills to bring new taxes for America's richest
articles.summary: California voters have recently rejected a proposed tax on billionaires.
articles.body: California voters have recently rejected a proposed tax on billionaires. Proposition 40, which sought a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, lost by roughly 53% to 47% following a campaign financed by wealthy opponents, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin. The measure would have directed most proceeds towards healthcare, with additional funding for education and food assistance. Brin contributed more than $100 million to Building a Better California, a political committee opposing the proposal. However, California’s rejection comes as five other states have adopted taxes targeting the richest.​Those measures differ from Proposition 40: they tax income above specified thresholds, rather than accumulated wealth such as shares and business holdings. Several are scheduled to take effect in 2027 or 2028, while others are already in place. Here’s what we know about these taxes:​What taxes five other states have or are planning for their richest​Massachusetts: Voters approved an additional 4% tax on income above $1 million in 2022, which became effective in 2023. The threshold rises with inflation and stands at $1,107,750 for the 2026 tax year. Revenue from this supports education and transportation in the state.​Hawaii: A new top personal income-tax rate of 13% will take effect in 2027. For married couples filing jointly, that rate applies to income above $1 million. The state’s tax department estimates that the change will generate an additional $53 million in 2027. The 13% figure is the applicable tax rate, rather than an additional 13% surcharge.​Maine: A 2% surcharge, which was set to start applying in 2027, has already taken effect in the 2026 tax year. It applies to taxable income above $1 million for single filers and $1.5 million for joint filers, heads of household, and surviving spouses.​Rhode Island: A surcharge on taxable income exceeding $1 million is set to begin at 1% in 2027, increase to 2% in 2028 and reach 3% in 2029. Once fully implemented, it raises the rate on income above that threshold from 5.99% to 8.99%.​Washington: Lawmakers enacted a 9.9% tax on Washington taxable income above $1 million, which is set to begin January 1, 2028. The first returns and payments covering that income will be due in 2029.​Why California’s billionaire tax faced opposition​California Governor Gavin Newsom was among the Democrats opposing the measure. Critics claimed that it could encourage wealthy residents to leave, weakening the state’s income-tax base.​Meanwhile, California’s Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated that the proposal could generate tens of billions of dollars over several years. It also warned of a possible continuing reduction of less than $1 billion annually in income-tax revenue as billionaires changed their behaviour. That was a potential fiscal consequence, rather than a confirmed loss.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.body: An 85-year-old Massachusetts man allegedly lost more than $1 million after being drawn into a romance and investment fraud scheme by a woman who falsely claimed she stood to inherit farmland in Brazil, federal prosecutors said.Maria Auxiliadora Rezende, 66, of Revere, Massachusetts, has been indicted on one count of wire fraud for allegedly deceiving the elderly man by claiming that she would inherit farmland in Brazil and that he could make a profit by helping her pay inheritance taxes and legal fees.How the alleged $1 million romance scam unfoldedAccording to the US Attorney's Office for the District of Massachusetts, Rezende allegedly entered into a romantic relationship with the victim, who had health and memory issues, before persuading him to send money towards the purported inheritance.However, prosecutors said the farmland, inheritance tax, lawyers and associated legal fees were all fictitious. The victim allegedly transferred more than $1 million to Rezende and her associates as part of the scheme.Rezende was arrested and charged through a criminal complaint on November 10, 2026. A federal grand jury subsequently indicted her on the wire fraud charge.If convicted, she faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison, up to three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000. The actual sentence would be determined by a federal district court judge, taking into account sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors.US Attorney Leah B Foley and Thomas Demeo, special agent in charge of the Internal Revenue Service's Criminal Investigation Boston Field Office, announced the indictment.The investigation also received assistance from Homeland Security Investigations in New England and the US Secret Service's Boston Field Office.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Ohio landlord put a departing couple's belongings on the curb, where strangers began going through them; on November 13, an appeals court upheld $5,790 in damages plus $7,223 in legal fees and costs
articles.summary: Moving out of a rental home can be stressful, but for one couple in Ohio, the end of their tenancy turned into an expensive legal battle after their
articles.body: Moving out of a rental home can be stressful, but for one couple in Ohio, the end of their tenancy turned into an expensive legal battle after their belongings were put outside for strangers to go through. What started as a dispute over a move-out deadline has ended up in an appeals court, which affirmed a decision that the landlords pay thousands of dollars in damages, attorney fees and court costs.Landlord puts couple’s stuff outsideThe case involved Jasmine and Charles Petties, who had lived in a residential property in Stark County, Ohio, since 2015, the Ohio Court of Appeals, Fifth District said. Charles signed a one-year lease initially, but then the lease went to month-to-month.In 2023, landlord Marvin Johnson put the property up for sale and offered Charles the opportunity to purchase it. The couple then began to make other accommodation arrangements when they found they could not afford to buy the home, the online data informs.Charles told Johnson in July 2023 he had found somewhere else and would move in September. But the two sides failed to agree on a mutually acceptable exit date.Johnson gave the couple a three-day notice Sept. 15 telling them to be out by the next day. On September 16 the couple started loading their belongings into a rental truck, with Johnson assisting in the process. The next day it escalated when Johnson told Charles the rest of his belongings would be put outside. The appellate court’s account says the possessions were moved to the curb and members of the public began going through them. Johnson then reached out to Jasmine and asked the couple to come pick up their stuff because people were trying to take it.Couple sues over damaged propertyJasmine went to the police in April 2024 before she filed a lawsuit. The complaint originally alleged unlawful landlord activity, trespass, negligence, civil conspiracy, and punitive damages. The trial court thereafter allowed an amendment to the complaint adding Charles as a co-plaintiff.Jasmine testified about several damaged or missing items at the bench trial in May 2025. Missing items included a broken treadmill, a damaged entertainment center and a backpack containing an Apple Watch and jewelry. She put the value of the damaged and missing items at a combined $5,790.The magistrate found the landlords were in violation of Ohio’s residential landlord-tenant law and awarded the couple $5,790 in compensatory damages. But the court dismissed their claims for trespassing and punitive damages.Appeals court rejects landlord's argumentsThe landlords appealed the decision on three grounds: that Charles should not have been added to the lawsuit, that the damages were miscalculated and that the award of attorney fees was wrong. The Ohio Court of Appeals, Fifth District, affirmed the lower court’s judgment in a November 13, 2026 ruling, rejecting all three arguments.The appeals court determined that adding Charles as a plaintiff was permissible because it added no new claims or defendants and did not unfairly prejudice the landlords.It further rejected the challenge to the award of damages, holding that the appellants had not challenged the magistrate's findings and had not provided a trial transcript necessary for review of their evidentiary arguments.also confirmed 7,223 inLegal fees and detailsThe landlords also challenged the award of attorney fees, claiming it was beyond the amount contemplated in the couple’s contingency-fee agreement with their attorney. The appellate court disagreed, finding that Ohio law permits tenants to recover reasonable attorney fees for landlord violations of the statutory protections. A private agreement between the client and the lawyer does not limit the amount that can be recovered from the landlord.The additional amount owed was $7,223, which included $6,700 in attorney fees and $523 in costs awarded by the lower courtAll three of the appellate challenges were rejected, and the judgment in Petties v. Johnson was affirmed. Therefore, the landlords were on the hook for the combined $13,013 in damages, legal fees and costs.Image Courtesy: istockYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Alaska sues GoFundMe and five other platforms, alleging 1.4 million charity fundraising pages were created without permission, including thousands linked to nonprofits across the state
articles.summary: Online fundraising has made it easier for people to contribute to charities, often through a few clicks on a crowdfunding website.
articles.body: Online fundraising has made it easier for people to contribute to charities, often through a few clicks on a crowdfunding website. But questions about who controls those appeals, and whether the organisations named in them have agreed to participate, have prompted legal action in Alaska. The state's Attorney General has filed lawsuits against six fundraising and charity-related platforms, including GoFundMe, alleging that they created donation pages in the names of nonprofits without obtaining their consent. The cases concern thousands of charities in Alaska and raise questions about how donations are collected, what information donors receive and how much money eventually reaches the organisations they intend to support.Alaska takes six crowdfunding platforms to court over charity donation pagesAlaska Attorney General Stephen Cox announced the legal action on March 10, 2026, naming GoFundMe, PayPal, Charity Navigator, JustGiving, Pledge to and Network for Good in the lawsuits. According to the state's allegations, the companies used information available in the public domain to set up fundraising pages representing nonprofit organisations, without first securing approval from those groups.The Attorney General's Office said the platforms had created pages for more than a million nonprofits, with several thousand organisations based in Alaska among those potentially affected. The state is seeking to establish whether the companies had the necessary authorisation to collect contributions using the identities of these organisations.Cox said, “Alaskans are generous people. But generosity depends on trust. GoFundMe and similar platforms used nonprofits’ good names to solicit donations without coordinating with the organizations actually doing the charitable work. That means some Alaskans may have donated thinking they were supporting a specific charity, when the charity never authorized the page and may never have received the donation—or may have received less than donors intended because of fees. Alaska law is clear: if you’re going to raise money in a charity’s name, you must first get the charity’s consent. These lawsuits are about protecting donors, protecting nonprofits, and preserving the public trust that makes charitable giving possible.”GoFundMe pages reportedly covered thousands of Alaska charitiesGoFundMe's activities formed a significant part of the state's investigation. As reported by the State of Alaska, in autumn 2025, the platform created approximately 1.4 million functioning fundraising pages associated with different charitable organisations, according to the Attorney General's announcement.As many as 5,000 Alaska-based charities may have had pages created in their names. The state said that, in most instances, the organisations had not been informed beforehand. The pages allowed individuals to make donations, raising questions about whether the nonprofits had agreed to the fundraising arrangements or knew that contributions were being collected under their names.The Consumer Protection Unit within the Attorney General's Office subsequently examined other platforms and identified similar arrangements. Investigators found donation pages that appeared to represent Alaska nonprofits, although the organisations concerned had not agreed to let the platforms solicit contributions on their behalf.The lawsuits therefore extend beyond GoFundMe. They cover six companies that the state identified among the major platforms involved in hosting or generating fundraising pages connected with Alaska charities.Why unauthorised fundraising pages have become a legal issueThe dispute centres on more than the appearance of a charity's name on a website. Nonprofits generally manage their own fundraising relationships, deciding which organisations they work with, what information they share with potential donors and how contributions are collected. A third-party page created without their involvement can leave them with limited control over those arrangements.The state has pointed to the possibility of platform fees reducing the amount received by a charity, as well as pages displaying information that is no longer accurate. In some cases, an independently created appeal could compete with a nonprofit's own fundraising campaign, making it harder for donors to distinguish between authorised and unauthorised requests.Access to donor information is another issue. When contributions pass through a platform without the charity's involvement, the organisation may not know who has given money or when the donation was made. That can affect its ability to acknowledge contributions, maintain donor records and communicate with supporters.The state has also raised concerns about transparency over how much of the money collected ultimately reaches the organisation named on the page. Even where a donation is made with a particular charity in mind, the arrangements governing its collection may not have been agreed with that charity.Why Alaska's nonprofit sector is concerned about third-party fundraisingThe lawsuits received support from The Foraker Group, an Alaska organisation established in 2001 to help nonprofits and tribes strengthen their internal operations and encourage philanthropy. Its president and chief executive, Laurie Wolf, said, “GoFundMe's unauthorized donation page and those like it on other platforms negatively impact the nonprofit sector.”The group's position reflects a wider concern raised in the cases: donors need to understand who is collecting their money, while charities should be able to determine how their identities are used in appeals for financial support. For nonprofits, the distinction between receiving a donation directly and having a third-party platform collect it can affect everything from financial reporting to communication with supporters. The state argues that these arrangements should not be established without the organisation's agreement.What Alaska is seeking through the lawsuitsThe Attorney General's Office has brought the cases under provisions of the Alaska Charitable Solicitations Act and the Alaska Consumer Protection Act. The state's position is that fundraising on behalf of a charity requires its consent, rather than simply relying on information about the organisation that is publicly available.The lawsuits seek court orders directing the companies to take down unauthorised donation pages associated with Alaska charities. The state is also pursuing civil penalties for alleged violations of the laws governing charitable fundraising and unfair trade practices.The proceedings will determine how the allegations are addressed and what obligations the platforms may have had when creating or hosting the pages. The announcement does not establish that every page identified by investigators resulted in a donation being misdirected or that every charity failed to receive money intended for it.You use AI every day. articles.title: A North Carolina woman says her stalker obtained her private Verizon records using fake police warrants and then threatened her life; a judge awarded her $18.6 million against him, not the phone company
articles.summary: A federal judge in North Carolina has ordered a convicted stalker to pay $18.632 million to a woman whose private phone records he obtained from Verizon
articles.body: A federal judge in North Carolina has ordered a convicted stalker to pay $18.632 million to a woman whose private phone records he obtained from Verizon using a fake search warrant. US District Judge Terrence W. Boyle issued the default judgment against 61-year-old Robert Michael Glauner in the Eastern District of North Carolina on 10 November 2026. The award includes $8,632,000 for the woman's pain, suffering and emotional distress, along with another $10 million in punitive damages. The judgment applies only to Glauner. The woman's separate legal claims against Verizon Communications Inc. and Verizon Wireless Services, LLC, have been put on hold while those disputes are handled through private arbitration.How the fake warrant workedAccording to court documents in the civil case, identified as M.D. v. Verizon Communications, Inc., the woman met Glauner online in August 2023. Her lawyer, Amanda Dure, told WRAL that the relationship "quickly soured". The woman then blocked Glauner on her personal mobile phone and online accounts. Court records and the UNC School of Government state that Glauner later pretended to be a detective with the Cary Police Department in North Carolina. He used a fake search warrant sent from a private email address to demand the woman's account information from Verizon.Verizon responded to the false request on 10 October 2023 and handed over her private information. This included her new telephone number and home address. After obtaining these details, Glauner began sexually harassing the woman, verbally abusing her and threatening to kill her. According to an FBI affidavit cited by 404 Media and ExtremeTech, he eventually travelled across the country from Albuquerque, New Mexico, to Raleigh, North Carolina, to confront her. Police arrested Glauner outside the woman's home on 6 November 2023. Officers found a knife and a rope inside his vehicle.Criminal conviction and lasting traumaFederal prosecutors charged Glauner with eight felony offences in January 2024. These included travelling across state lines with the intention of killing, injuring or harassing someone. The US Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of North Carolina said Glauner pleaded guilty to all eight charges on 10 April 2025. The charges included stalking and aggravated identity theft. He was sentenced to 65 months in federal prison. According to Bureau of Prisons records cited in the court order, he is currently held at FCI Lompoc I in California. His scheduled release date is 6 November 2027.In a victim impact statement submitted during the criminal proceedings, the woman described how the incident destroyed her sense of safety. Her words were quoted in Judge Boyle's November 2026 order. "In October of 2023, my stalker, Robert Glauner, fraudulently obtained all of my personal information from my phone company, Verizon. I have not known a moment of peace since then. I still cannot believe that this happened ... My life is so different since this happened," she told the court. She also explained how Glauner's repeated phone calls to her workplace affected her job and physical health. "By April of 2024, my physical health matched my mental health, and I could no longer physically work at the store .... the anxiety and PTSD are so severe that it's hard to function .... I want to wake up from this nightmare, from this world where someone would threaten to kill me, to take me away from my family and my friends, because if he 'could not have me, no one else could,'" she stated.Calculating the $18.6 million awardA forensic psychological evaluation completed on 1 April 2026 found that the woman was suffering from several mental health conditions. Dr. Moore diagnosed her with post-traumatic stress disorder, adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depression, and somatoform disorder. In his report, which was quoted in the court's decision, Dr. Moore said her trauma reactions "have notably undermined her social functioning, reduced her adaptive functioning, and apparently have negatively impacted her physical functioning with a potential onset of psychogenic seizures".Glauner did not respond to the civil lawsuit filed in August 2024. This allowed the woman to ask the court for a default judgment, which can be issued when a defendant fails to respond to a case. Under North Carolina law, Judge Boyle allowed damages for pain and suffering to be calculated on a daily basis. Court records show that the woman had experienced 916 days of documented trauma between the October 2023 data breach and her April 2026 court filing.The judge also considered Glauner's remaining life expectancy. Using state mortality tables, the court found that a 61-year-old man has an estimated remaining life expectancy of 20.4 years, or 7,446 days. During that period, the woman faces a credible fear of retaliation when Glauner is released from prison. Judge Boyle approved the requested $8.632 million in compensation for her suffering. He then added $10 million in punitive damages, pointing to Glauner's "unconscionable behavior". This brought the total award to $18.632 million.Why Verizon is not payingThe woman initially filed a lawsuit against both Glauner and Verizon. She accused them of violating the federal Stored Communications Act and causing emotional distress. However, Verizon will not be required to pay under the latest court judgment. Its part of the dispute is being handled separately through private arbitration. In September 2025, Judge Boyle approved Verizon's request to separate its part of the lawsuit and move the claims into private arbitration.The decision was based on an arbitration clause in Verizon's standard customer agreement, which the woman signed when she opened her wireless account in June 2023. The woman argued that the federal Ending Forced Arbitration of Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Act prevented Verizon from enforcing that clause. She said the case involved serious sexual harassment by Glauner. Judge Boyle rejected that argument in relation to the telecom company. As a result, the woman's claims against Verizon will continue through private arbitration rather than a public court trial. The $18.632 million judgment therefore applies only to Glauner. He remains in federal prison, with his scheduled release set for late 2027.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US returns 337 looted antiquities to Italy after major investigations; collection includes a marble head of Alexander the Great stolen from a Rome museum in 1960
articles.summary: The United States has returned 337 looted antiquities to Italy, in one of the largest recent returns of stolen cultural property, according to Reuters.
articles.body: The United States has returned 337 looted antiquities to Italy, in one of the largest recent returns of stolen cultural property, according to Reuters. The objects were presented on Wednesday, 29 April 2026, at the headquarters of the Carabinieri cultural protection unit in Rome. They include Roman, Greek, Etruscan and Egyptian pieces, handed back after investigations, many of them centred on New York. Among the most significant is a first-century AD marble head of Alexander the Great, stolen from a Rome museum in 1960. Reuters reports that the Manhattan District Attorney’s office found 221 of the objects, and that the recovered items will now be studied.337 looted antiquities return to Italy after US-led investigationsAccording to Reuters, the 337 artefacts were returned by the United States following a series of investigations, many of them centred on New York. Reuters reports that the items range from ancient Roman sculptures to Greek, Etruscan and Egyptian pieces. The agency says the handover highlighted closer cooperation between Rome and Washington. It adds that the Manhattan District Attorney's office found 221 of the objects in this latest haul.Reuters reports that the US Ambassador to Italy, Tilman J. Fertitta, told reporters that the United States would do whatever it takes to help bring such artefacts back to Italy. Italian Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli also spoke at the presentation. He said that protecting cultural heritage means defending memory and strengthening identity, and that it passes the value of culture on to future generations as a universal public good.Alexander the Great marble head stolen from a Rome museum in 1960Reuters names the marble head of Alexander the Great as one of the most significant items unveiled. It dates to the first century AD and was stolen from a Rome museum in 1960. Reuters lists other notable pieces: a bronze sculpture looted from the Roman town of Herculaneum and two Egyptian basalt statues. The recovered objects also include Roman coins, jewellery, ceramics and architectural fragments spanning the fifth century BC to the third century AD.The Manhattan District Attorney's Office describes a first-century C.E. marble head depicting Alexander the Great as Helios, the sun god, in a press release dated 6 August 2025. According to the office, the head was excavated from the Basilica Emilia in the Roman Forum and stolen from the Antiquarium Forense Museum, a state-run archaeological museum in Rome. The release says it was laundered through several individuals and institutions in New York. Alan Safani acquired it in good faith in 2017. The office seized it under a warrant, and Safani eventually agreed to surrender it so it could be repatriated.Manhattan investigations trace stolen Italian antiquities to trafficking networksAccording to the Manhattan District Attorney's Office, the objects in its August 2025 announcement were recovered through criminal investigations into several antiquities trafficking networks. The office names convicted traffickers Giacomo Medici, Giovanni Franco Becchina, Robin Symes, Robert Hecht and Eugene Alexander, as well as alleged trafficker Edoardo Almagià. It says Alexander was convicted on 8 July 2025 of Conspiracy in the Fifth Degree to Commit Antiquities Trafficking. It also says it holds an arrest warrant for Almagià, who is awaiting extradition from Italy.The office's release gives further examples of items repatriated to Italy on 5 August 2025, part of a group of 31 antiquities. These include 61 fragments of a terracotta column-krater attributed to the Lydos Painter and dated to 580 B.C.E. The Antiquities Trafficking Unit seized them from the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2025. The release says smugglers broke the object into fragments and sold the pieces separately over several years. The Unit also seized nine Tarentine objects from the Met in 2025. The office says they date to the 4th and 3rd centuries B.C.E. and come from tombs in southern Italy. Of one group of seven, it notes that the only provenance was the "English collection".Italy strengthens efforts to recover stolen artefacts from USItaly has spent decades trying to curb a rampant trade in illicitly excavated antiquities. In that time, it has secured the return of thousands of artefacts worth tens of millions of euros. According to the agency, the campaign has gained momentum in recent years, helped by online databases, advances in technology and closer cooperation with US authorities. Reuters adds that Italy and the United States renewed a memorandum of understanding last year. It tightens US import restrictions on Italian archaeological material, strengthens customs controls and expands information-sharing.The United States is one of the main markets for global antiquities, with auction houses, private collectors and museums interested in rare artefacts. An Italian Culture Ministry official who was not authorised to speak to the press said, "We know what is missing and are getting much better at finding it." She predicted more returns in future. Reuters also reports that the recovered objects will now be studied and, where possible, returned to their places of origin across Italy. The Manhattan District Attorney's Office says its Antiquities Trafficking Unit has recovered more than 6,060 antiquities since its creation, valued at more than $476 million. It says it has returned more than 5,700 of them to 30 countries.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Two live snakes found inside passenger's suitcase at California airport: 'When I realized the item in my hand was alive...'
articles.summary: Transportation Security Administration officers at a California airport were in for a shocking surprise after discovering two live snakes concealed inside
articles.body: Transportation Security Administration officers at a California airport were in for a shocking surprise after discovering two live snakes concealed inside a passenger's suitcase during a routine security inspection. One of the reptiles was identified as a rattlesnake, prompting officials to temporarily suspend security screening over safety concerns.The unusual discovery was made at Ontario International Airport in Southern California in October, according to the TSA. Officers were inspecting a checked bag when an X-ray scan revealed what initially appeared to be a rope inside the luggage. When TSA Officer Benjamin Andrade-Carillo examined the item more closely, he realized it was moving. "When I realized the item in my hand was alive, I told myself, 'I need to escalate this immediately,'" Andrade-Carillo told CBS Los Angeles.He immediately alerted his supervisors, who joined the inspection. Supervisory TSA Officer Suggey Flores said he felt the pillowcase tighten and begin moving when he handled it. "I have held snakes before, so I wasn't too spooked. I was more impressed, because it's not something you see every day," Flores said.Officials discovered that there were two live snakes inside the pillowcase. One of them was a rattlesnake, according to the TSA.Airport security screening temporarily haltedThe discovery prompted TSA officers to temporarily pause security screening in the immediate area as they assessed the potential danger posed by the reptiles. Officials said they initially did not know what species the snakes belonged to or whether they were venomous. "Safety was a concern because we didn't know what kind of snakes they were. They could have been venomous," Flores said.'They are my pets'Airport police were alerted and took possession of the luggage before bringing it to the airline's ticketing area, where they located the passenger. The traveller reportedly told officials that the snakes were his pets and that he had previously flown with them on another airline. He removed the reptiles from the suitcase and handed them over to a family member who was not travelling. TSA officers then screened the suitcase again and cleared it for travel. The passenger was allowed to board his flight without the snakes.No one was injured or bitten during the incident, and normal security operations resumed.Andrade-Carillo said he had never encountered anything similar during his two years with the agency. "In my two years of service, I had not found anything like this," he said. He recalled another unusual incident in San Diego in which a passenger attempted to carry live lobsters through airport security.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Michigan woman was owed more than $1 million after her ex-husband died with 84 divorce-settlement payments outstanding; on November 13, judges revived her lawsuit against the lawyer who drafted the deal
articles.summary: Jamie Lee Baker’s divorce settlement promised her $13,000 a month for 111 months, secured by assignments of her former husband’s interests in several
articles.body: Jamie Lee Baker’s divorce settlement promised her $13,000 a month for 111 months, secured by assignments of her former husband’s interests in several limited liability companies. When Kevin Baker died after making only 27 payments, 84 payments worth more than $1 million remained outstanding, and Jamie discovered that much of the collateral behind the agreement may not have been what she thought it was. On November 13, the Michigan Court of Appeals reversed a lower court’s dismissal of her legal malpractice lawsuit against attorney Michael A. Robbins, according to the Justia U.S Law case record.The ruling does not decide whether Robbins was negligent. It does, however, send the case back for further proceedings after finding that there were genuine issues of material fact about whether the assignments in the divorce settlement actually provided the security Jamie was promised.What the settlement promisedJamie and Kevin Baker’s divorce settlement included property settlement payments of $13,000 per month for 111 months. To protect her if Kevin stopped paying, the agreement called for assignments of his membership interests in several LLCs, including LIP GTC, LIP LIMA, LIP Auburn, LIP Cascade, LIP Hall Road Crossing Holdings, and LIP Madison.Kevin was a real estate broker and investor. During the divorce, he provided a list of 14 LLCs in which he claimed membership interests and indicated that LIP Holdings owned five of those interests.The problem was that five of the entities listed as collateral were actually owned by LIP Holdings, not by Kevin directly. Kevin held his interest in LIP Cascade directly, but he did not assign his interest in LIP Holdings itself as part of the settlement.What happened after his deathAfter the divorce was finalised, Kevin made 27 monthly payments before he died. That left 84 payments outstanding, totaling more than $1 million.Jamie then tried to collect on the collateral through probate proceedings. The probate court found that the assignment of Kevin’s 80 percent interest in LIP Cascade was valid and binding, and ordered that interest to be assigned to Jamie.But for the other five LLCs, the court discovered that LIP Holdings, not Kevin, owned the entities. That meant Kevin did not have personal membership interests in those companies that he could assign directly to Jamie.The complication with LIP HoldingsLIP Holdings’ operating agreement included an involuntary transfer provision. If a member’s interest was subject to an involuntary transfer, the other member, in this case the Daniel Kukes Living Trust, had the option to purchase that interest for 50 percent of its book value.The Kukes Trust argued that the probate court’s order and the underlying assignment triggered that provision. It offered $137,244 to purchase any membership interests Jamie claimed to hold in the LIP entities.Jamie eventually settled with the Kukes Trust for $235,000 in exchange for her purported membership interests. Even after adding $194,000 from the sale of LIP Cascade, the total she received from the collateral was less than half of what Kevin still owed under the divorce settlement.What Jamie allegesJamie sued Robbins for legal malpractice, arguing that he failed to obtain sufficient security and collateral under the divorce settlement. She also alleged that he failed to recognise and advise her about the consequences of the assignments, and failed to involve the Kukes Trust during the assignment process.To succeed on a legal malpractice claim in Michigan, Jamie must show that an attorney-client relationship existed, that Robbins was negligent, that the negligence caused her injury, and that she suffered actual damages. The appeals court found that the trial court’s dismissal was premature because there were factual questions that needed to be resolved.The court noted that the husband had no personal membership interests in the five LIP entities, since those entities were wholly owned by LIP Holdings. It also noted that a member of an LLC has no interest in specific LLC property, which means Kevin could not simply assign the entities themselves as collateral.Why the appeals court reversedThe trial court had granted summary disposition, finding that Jamie did receive the specific collateral she bargained for. The appeals court disagreed, saying that conclusion was based on an incorrect legal premise.The probate court’s orders recognised the LIP entities as non-probate assets, but they did not actually assign interests in those entities by operation of law. The appeals court said those orders did not address whether Kevin had any interest in the entities in the first place, or how his interest in LIP Holdings factored into the assignments.Because Kevin had no personal membership interests in the five LIP entities, the appeals court found that the trial court erred in concluding that Jamie had validly assigned any membership interests in those entities. That error meant the case could not be dismissed at that stage.What happens nextThe appeals court reversed the grant of summary disposition and remanded the case for further proceedings. It noted that the lawsuit is still at an early stage, and that either party may seek summary disposition again after discovery is complete.For Jamie, the ruling means her malpractice claim is alive. She can now pursue discovery and try to prove that Robbins’s handling of the settlement caused her to lose collateral that was supposed to protect her financially.For Robbins, the case is not yet decided. The appeals court did not find that he was negligent, it simply found that there were factual questions that needed to be answered before the case could be dismissed.The case is important becauseThis case shows the importance of knowing exactly what is being transferred as security in a divorce settlement.However, LLC interest is different from LLC asset, and a member cannot transfer property owned by the LLC that is not owned by the member.It also shows how operating agreements can complicate things. Even if an assignment is valid on paper, an involuntary transfer provision can limit what a former spouse can actually receive.Jamie still doesn’t know how it will turn out. But the appeals court’s decision gives her a chance to have her claims heard, and it underscores the importance of careful legal drafting when large sums of money and complex business interests are involved.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2008, Brandi Carlile founded the Looking Out Foundation with her bandmates; 18 years later, its grants have passed $10 million and a 2026 award recognises its impact
articles.summary: Singer Brandi Carlile has been named Entertainer of the Year at the 2026 Anthem Awards.
articles.body: Singer Brandi Carlile has been named Entertainer of the Year at the 2026 Anthem Awards. The recognition comes after the charity she started with her bandmates passed $10 million in grants to organisations supporting communities in need. The International Academy of Digital Arts and Sciences announced the winners of the 6th Annual Anthem Awards in New York on 5 November 2026. Judges selected Carlile for a Special Achievement Award in recognition of her work supporting LGBTQ+ equality and raising millions of dollars for grassroots organisations through the Looking Out Foundation. Carlile founded the Seattle-based non-profit in 2008 with her longtime bandmates, Tim and Phil Hanseroth. The organisation encourages concertgoers and music fans to support charitable causes through donations. According to the Looking Out Foundation, it has distributed more than $10 million across the United States and other parts of the world. Much of this money has come from campaigns where the average donation is just $25.How small fan donations drive global grantsInstead of depending only on large companies and corporate sponsors, the Looking Out Foundation raises money directly from music fans at concerts and through music releases. The charity works with volunteers and local groups to collect donations for causes that often find it difficult to receive funding from larger organisations. According to the foundation's official records, its grants support LGBTQIA2S+ communities, disadvantaged young people, public health programmes, women's empowerment, the arts, food banks and housing projects. It also provides emergency funding to help children and families living in areas affected by war. The foundation has supported hundreds of local and international organisations. In the arts and youth music sector, its grant recipients include MusiCares, Girls Rock Camp ATL, Seattle Youth Symphony and the Americana Music Association Foundation. For community development and hunger relief, the charity has provided funding to UNICEF, the World Food Programme and Meals on Wheels America. It has also supported regional food banks in New York, Los Angeles, Denver and Seattle. Its grants for health and civil rights work have reached organisations such as the Campaign for Southern Equality, The Queer Trans Project and the Oklahoma Birth Equity Initiative.Leadership and board structureCarlile and brothers Tim and Phil Hanseroth continue to serve on the Looking Out Foundation's board of directors. They work alongside board chair Catherine Carlile and board member Xiomara Padamsee. The charity's daily operations are managed by executive director Gloria Goeres. She joined the organisation in 2024 after previously working as executive director of Together Rising. Goeres works with communications and volunteer manager Kate McNicholas, who joined in 2025, and grants and research manager Sami Narayanan. Narayanan moved into a staff position in 2026 after first volunteering with the foundation. The Looking Out Foundation has received a four-star rating from independent charity evaluator Charity Navigator.Recognition at the 2026 Anthem AwardsThe Anthem Awards are presented by The Webby Awards and recognise campaigns that make a difference in society. They cover seven main areas, including human rights, health, education and humanitarian work. Organisers said the 2026 awards attracted more than 2,500 entries from 43 countries. Carlile was among several people recognised with Special Achievement Awards this year. Seth and Lauren Miller Rogen were named Advocates of the Year for their Alzheimer's charity, Hilarity for Charity. WNBA Players Association president Nneka Ogwumike received the Athlete of the Year award. Podcast host Jay Shetty and business leaders David and Michael Bronner also received Special Achievement honours.Gold Anthem Award winners across the wider categories included Doctors Without Borders, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research, The Rockefeller Foundation, World Wildlife Fund and PFLAG National. In the Anthem Awards press release, general manager Patricia McLoughlin spoke about how this year's winners continued their work despite a difficult period for non-profit organisations. "Across the board this year, we saw a sector bouncing back from an extremely difficult 2025 with creativity and resolve," McLoughlin said. "From grassroots nonprofits to global brands, this year's Winners are finding new pathways for impact, like using humor to spread their message and stepping into technology to reach more people, all while staying steadfast in their mission to make the world better. Join me in congratulating the Winners of the 6th Annual Anthem Awards for setting a new standard for good."The event also included a Community Voice Celebration, where members of the public voted for their favourite finalists. More than 67,000 votes were cast. The finalists selected by the public included Girls Who Code, the Innocence Project and Refugees International. For Carlile and her bandmates, the 2026 award marks 18 years since they first began asking fans at small club concerts to donate a few dollars to local shelters and community organisations. The foundation continues to follow the same approach. It believes that small donations can make a major difference when collected from large numbers of people during concert tours. Through campaigns with an average donation of $25, the Looking Out Foundation continues to direct money towards organisations working directly with communities in need.You use AI every day. articles.title: Unable to take care, 67-year-old man strangles 85-year-old mom to death in Kolkata, calls cops
articles.summary: Kolkata engineer, 67, allegedly strangles 85-year-old mother in Haridevpur, cites financial hardship and caregiving strain; calls police to confess, arrested.
articles.body: KOLKATA: A 67-year-old engineer, jobless since Covid, allegedly strangled her 85-year-old mother to death at their Haridevpur home on Monday morning as he was unable to take care of her. He then called the police emergency helpline — 100 — and confessed to the crime.Sagar Ghosh told police that he had been “out of any meaningful work” since the pandemic and was “unable to take care of his ailing mother due to his advanced age”.The accused wrote in a note to his sister, who lived with him but was not at home when their mother was killed, “I have let mother go. I have freed her. When you return home, you won’t find me either.”Sagar, who neighbours said has been struggling financially since losing his job, has been arrested.Police said the accused strangled his mother, Uma Rani Ghosh, with a white thread around 11am on the first floor of their house on Hafiz Mohammad Ishaq Road, near Behala’s Sodepur.Additional commissioner of police (I) Dip Narayan Goswami said, “The accused called up 100 and informed us about the matter. He was detained by local police and jointly questioned by the homicide section... before being arrested. Fingerprint and photography teams have collected evidence.”A preliminary investigation revealed that Uma Rani Ghosh, the victim, had been ailing for a long time, an officer said.Deputy commissioner of police (Behala) Ishani Paul said Sagar cited his inability to afford his mother’s medical and daily expenses as the trigger for his drastic decision to kill her. “It was mainly because of his old age that he was unable to look after his mother,” Paul said.Sagar lived on the first floor of the house with his mother and sister. The ground floor, also owned by them, has been rented out. Sagar’s wife and their son and daughter-in-law live elsewhere. The wife told police that she decided to live separately after Sagar allegedly hit her on her head with a hammer in 2020-21.Officers suspect the accused waited until his sister stepped out before killing their mother. “The sister left home at 9 am and returned close to noon, only to find her mother murdered,” an officer said.Forensic experts are verifying whether the note addressed to his sister was penned by Sagar.Neighbours said Sagar became reclusive after his wife left him. His speech and behavior appeared erratic frequently. At times, he would step out for walks with his mother. “He looked rather disturbed, more than his mother,” said Saikat Naha, a resident of the locality.“We are questioning the accused to know the motive behind the murder. articles.title: A Canadian farmer cut down a 2,000-foot line of mature trees on his neighbour's 40-acre property and filled a drainage ditch; a court ordered him to pay more than $213,000
articles.summary: In August and September 2012, Timothy Mullen entered his neighbour’s 40-acre property in Tilbury, Ontario, cut down a mature tree line of approximately
articles.body: In August and September 2012, Timothy Mullen entered his neighbour’s 40-acre property in Tilbury, Ontario, cut down a mature tree line of approximately 2,000 feet and filled in the drainage ditch beside it. The trees had separated the two farms. The court later found he did not have permission from the owner, Judith Ann Murphy. In 2018, the Ontario Superior Court held the defendants liable for trespass, and in 2020 it ordered them to pay $213,471.27 in damages. The Court of Appeal for Ontario dismissed their appeal in December 2021 and awarded Mrs Murphy costs of $20,000, all inclusive.How the removal of the 2,000-foot tree line affected the neighbouring farmAccording to the 2020 reasons for judgment of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, the Murphy property is 40 acres, and the Mullen property is 48 acres. A row of trees and a ditch ran along the west side of the Murphy property, between the two farms. The court described the tree line as "approximately 2,000 feet long", running from the south end of the property at Highway 46 to an old railroad track at the north end. Mrs Murphy said it included trees of roughly 40 to 60 feet tall. The Court of Appeal for Ontario later described the line of trees as approximately 2,000 feet long and 60 feet deep, with the drainage ditch on the Murphy property.The 2020 judgment states that the tree line provided a sound and light barrier from a residential subdivision to the west, a wind break and a visual screen between the two properties, and "a home for various wildlife". Mr Mullen bought his property in December 2010. According to the judgment, the land had no subsurface drainage, and he told the court, "I needed drainage on my property." The Court of Appeal records that he entered the Murphy property, cut and removed the trees, and then filled in the ditch. In cross-examination, quoted in the 2018 ruling, he agreed that the entire tree line was removed. Mrs Murphy first learned of the removal in September 2012, when her son Jason attended the property.Why the court ruled the tree cutting was unauthorisedThe plaintiffs asked for summary judgment on liability for trespass, and Justice Pamela Hebner heard the motion on 8 January 2018. In her ruling of 10 July 2018, she noted that Mr Mullen admitted entering the property, cutting trees and levelling the ditch, so the issue was whether he had permission. Both parties pointed to a telephone call of 3 August 2012, which Mrs Murphy's phone records showed lasted 16 minutes. Mrs Murphy said Mr Mullen told her he wanted to clean out the ditch and put in a new one, and that she asked to meet at the Comber Fair the following week to discuss it further. Mr Mullen said she agreed "as long as I saved her an oak log so she could make furniture out of it."Justice Hebner found the evidence "consistent overall with a discussion as opposed to an agreement". She noted that the meeting at the fair did not take place, because Mr Mullen did not go, and that Mr Mullen went onto the property the Friday after the fair. Mr Mullen had said that Mr Ian Pierce heard the call on speakerphone, but no affidavit from Mr Pierce was provided. The judge drew an adverse inference that he would not have supported Mr Mullen's version. She also wrote that the burden of proving leave and licence lay with Mr Mullen and that he had not met it. She granted judgment on liability and set a hearing on damages.Why the judge awarded more than $213,000 in damagesThe damages hearing took place on 20 and 21 March and 5 and 6 September 2019, and the reasons were released on 26 February 2020. Mrs Murphy asked for $1,214,396, made up of $714,396 in special damages, $250,000 for loss of amenities and $250,000 in punitive damages. The defendants proposed $5,000, the cost of planting seedlings. Mrs Murphy's arborist, Philip van Wassenaer, proposed 431 replacement trees along the full length of the former tree line, plus 50 poplar whips, at a total of $221,706. He also gave costs of $37,800 plus HST for irrigation and $39,750 plus HST for a deer fence. The judge applied the approach from the British Columbia case Kates v. Hall: the amount needed to pay for the remedial work that a reasonable person in the plaintiff's position, without monetary constraints, would carry out. She accepted that Mrs Murphy intended to build a home on the southwest corner of the property, and found that a reasonable person would plant along one third of the 610-metre former hedge row, or approximately 200 metres.On that basis, the judge used one third of the arborist's planting figure, $73,902, and assessed $20,000 for irrigation and $13,000 for fencing, giving $106,902 for restoration. She added $31,569.27 in out-of-pocket expenses, which included a survey that cost $6,440.59 and the cost of a municipal drain. The Court of Appeal records that the drain cost $102,000 in total under the Drainage Act, with $77,032 assessed to the Mullen property and $24,968 to the Murphy property. For loss of amenities, the judge took half of the 300 trees Mrs Murphy's son had counted, which was 150 trees. She wrote that there was "some precedent" for $1,000 per tree but reduced it to $500 because there was no house on the property yet, giving $75,000. The total was $213,471.27. She declined to award punitive damages, finding the defendant's conduct "reckless" but not high-handed enough to deserve rebuke.Why the Ontario Court of Appeal upheld the $213,000 damages awardThe defendants appealed, and the Court of Appeal for Ontario heard the case by video conference on 20 September 2021. Justice Alexandra Hoy wrote the decision, with Justices Rouleau and Thorburn agreeing. According to the decision, the appellants did not contest liability but challenged the amount of damages, and the court grouped their arguments into four categories: foreseeability, Mrs Murphy's intention to build a house and her affinity for trees, drainage, and other arguments. The court said it could interfere only if the trial judge erred in law, misapprehended the evidence or made a "palpably incorrect" or "wholly erroneous" assessment. On the drainage argument, it noted that the appellants called no expert evidence on whether the trees would have had to be removed anyway. On the number of trees, it noted that the expert's 480 replacement trees were much smaller than the original trees, so a larger number was needed to create an equivalent screen within a reasonable period.The court also found there was evidence supporting the trial judge's acceptance of the deer fence, and it described the 200-metre length and the $75,000 amenities figure as "far from arbitrary". It concluded that the appellants had not identified any reviewable error and that the assessment was not palpably incorrect or wholly erroneous. The appeal was dismissed, with costs to Mrs Murphy of $20,000, all inclusive. The decision was released on 9 December 2021.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Amid China rivalry, India joins move to shield AI tech chain
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India has joined United States and eight other Pax Silica initiative partners in signing the San Francisco Declaration to jointly protect
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India has joined United States and eight other Pax Silica initiative partners in signing the San Francisco Declaration to jointly protect critical infrastructure and supply chains essential for artificial intelligence (AI).The declaration is an international agreement that is being seen as an attempt to protect the full technology chain needed to build AI - from essential raw materials to manufacturing and energy networks.Amid intensifying rivalry with China, the agreement reinforces the importance of coordinated efforts to address economic coercion, supply chain disruptions, and non-market policies and practices and their market-distorting effects, while protecting private investment and ensuring a level playing field for innovation and growth.It treats the hardware, digital systems and logistics powering AI as vital national assets that partner countries must protect together for "economic security and enduring prosperity".Pax Silica is State Department's flagship effort on AI, renamed Super Intelligence or SI by President Donald Trump, and supply chain security, advancing new economic security consensus among allies and trusted partners."We affirm that the safeguarding of these sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure is a shared endeavour; that the security of each participant is strengthened by the vigilance of all; and that we engage in this common cause as aligned partners - in defense of prosperity and independence of our peoples," said the declaration.India joined US-led Pax Silica initiative in Feb this year, as both sides hailed a growing geopolitical consensus that "economic security is national security, and national security is economic security".State Department had then said India brings to Pax Silica a deep talent pool, processing and refining capacity for critical minerals, investments in AI infrastructure and an understanding of the importance of trusted technologies.The declaration was signed at a meeting of the founders of Pax Silica initiative convened by US Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg Sunday. It was released by govts of US, Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, UAE and UK.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A French woman who lost €830,000 to someone impersonating Brad Pitt takes two banks to court; she alleges they approved suspicious transfers despite bizarre payment descriptions
articles.summary: A French woman who lost €830,000 to scammers impersonating the actor Brad Pitt has filed a complaint against two banks, according to Riviera Radio, citing
articles.body: A French woman who lost €830,000 to scammers impersonating the actor Brad Pitt has filed a complaint against two banks, according to Riviera Radio, citing France Télévisions. Anne Deneuchatel accuses the banks of approving 18 payments carrying unusual references linked to a supposed kidney operation for the actor, without questioning them. The BBC reported in January 2025 that the scam began on Instagram in February 2023, and that she was sent multiple AI-generated photos of “Pitt” in a hospital bed. Her divorce settlement of €775,000 went entirely to the scammers. A police investigation is now under way, the BBC added.Banks face scrutiny over 18 payments linked to the alleged kidney surgery scamAccording to Riviera Radio, she says the banks approved 18 payments with unusual references linked to a supposed kidney operation for the Hollywood actor. Her claim therefore rests on the wording attached to the transfers as well as on their size.Asia Economy reports that the remittance memos contained descriptions such as "William Bradley Pitt kidney transplant", using Brad Pitt's real name. Korea's FN News, citing BFM TV and other outlets, says the references included the phrase "William Bradley Pitt surgery". According to Asia Economy, she argues that the banks must be held accountable and that there are loopholes in the system.How the fake Brad Pitt romance began through Instagram messagesAccording to the BBC, Anne, then 53 and an interior designer, downloaded Instagram in February 2023, when she was still married to a wealthy entrepreneur. She was contacted by someone who said they were Pitt's mother, Jane Etta. A person purporting to be Pitt got in touch the next day. The BBC reports that "Pitt" later said he had tried to send her luxury gifts but could not pay customs on them because his bank accounts were frozen during divorce proceedings with the actor Angelina Jolie. Anne transferred €9,000.The BBC says the requests for money increased when the fake Pitt claimed he needed cash for kidney cancer treatment, and sent her multiple AI-generated photos of Pitt in a hospital bed. Anne and her husband divorced, and she was awarded €775,000, all of which the BBC says went to the scammers. After scammers tried to obtain more money under the guise of "Special FBI Agent John Smith", Anne contacted the police, according to the BBC.French authorities investigate fraudsters behind the fake Brad Pitt identityA police investigation is under way. Gulf Today, reporting in January 2025, said that authorities in La Réunion had launched a probe to identify the fraudsters, and that police were trying to locate the accounts that received her transfers. The same report says she had lodged her complaint on the island, according to a police source.The BBC reported on 15 January 2025 that Anne's story drew a wave of mockery online, and that the French broadcaster TF1 withdrew a programme about her after her testimony sparked what it called "a wave of harassment". A representative for Pitt told Entertainment Weekly that it was "awful that scammers take advantage of fans' strong connection with celebrities", the BBC reports.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2022, The Weeknd began a worldwide stadium tour; four years and 176 concerts later, the shows have generated $8.5 million for humanitarian causes, with $3 million raised during 2026 alone
articles.summary: The Weeknd’s record-breaking stadium tour has left behind a legacy that extends well beyond music, raising millions of dollars for humanitarian causes
articles.body: The Weeknd’s record-breaking stadium tour has left behind a legacy that extends well beyond music, raising millions of dollars for humanitarian causes while drawing more than nine million fans worldwide. The singer’s After Hours Til Dawn Stadium Tour, which concluded in November 2026, generated $8.5 million for charitable initiatives supporting hunger relief and education, according to announcements by Live Nation, Billboard Canada and music publication XXL. Of the total amount, $3 million was raised in 2026 alone through contributions benefiting the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) and Global Citizen. The latest fundraising effort also includes support for initiatives aimed at improving healthcare, education and economic opportunities for women and girls. The four-year tour began in July 2022 and concluded with a final performance in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, on November 4. Across its remarkable run, the production covered 67 cities in 30 countries and five continents, completing 176 shows and selling more than nine million tickets.A record-breaking tour with a humanitarian impactThe charitable contributions were made through the XO Humanitarian Fund and Global Citizen, with the funds directed towards addressing global hunger and improving access to quality education for children. The 2026 contributions have also helped support a Global Citizen campaign focused on reducing barriers faced by women and girls, particularly in healthcare, education and economic participation.The initiative aims to encourage commitments that can create better opportunities for women and girls and help address inequalities affecting their access to essential services and resources. The Weeknd, whose real name is Abel Tesfaye, has maintained a connection with humanitarian work beyond the stadium tour. As a Global Ambassador for the United Nations World Food Programme, he has previously supported emergency food assistance in Ethiopia with a $2 million contribution. He also donated $4.5 million towards providing more than 18 million loaves of bread to families in Gaza through the XO Humanitarian Fund. According to his representatives, his charitable contributions across various causes have exceeded $12.6 million since 2020.The tour also makes music historyAlongside its charitable achievements, the After Hours Til Dawn Stadium Tour has set a major milestone in the global live music industry. With reported earnings exceeding $1.3 billion, it has become the highest-grossing concert tour by a male solo artist in history, surpassing Elton John’s Farewell Yellow Brick Road tour, which generated approximately $939 million.The tour also ranks among the three highest-grossing concert tours worldwide, behind Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour and Coldplay’s Music of the Spheres World Tour. Its final year was particularly successful, generating more than $500 million in ticket sales in 2026 alone, with over three million tickets sold. Several performances also set venue records, including seven shows at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium and six nights at Toronto’s Rogers Centre.The Asian leg brought another milestone, with four sold-out performances in Hong Kong attracting nearly 200,000 fans. The tour eventually closed in Kuala Lumpur after four years of performances across multiple continents.From record-breaking ticket sales to millions raised for humanitarian work, The Weeknd’s global stadium run has become one of the most commercially successful tours in music history while also directing a significant part of its impact towards communities in need.You use AI every day. articles.title: A US father spent over 25 years searching for his daughter after her mother took her to Mexico in 1999; a DNA test finally confirmed her identity, bringing them back into contact
articles.summary: A US father who spent more than 25 years searching for his missing daughter has finally reconnected with her after DNA testing confirmed her identity.
articles.body: A US father who spent more than 25 years searching for his missing daughter has finally reconnected with her after DNA testing confirmed her identity. Andrea Reyes was nearly two years old when her mother, Rosa Tenorio, took her to Mexico during a scheduled visit in 1999. Her father, Carlos Reyes-Couvertier, had legal custody of the child and reported her disappearance to the police.Despite investigations and several trips to Mexico, he could not bring his daughter home. According to The Associated Press, the case remained unresolved for years until a New Haven detective reopened it in 2023. The investigation led authorities to a woman living in Puebla, Mexico, whose DNA was later matched with her father's. The two have since spoken by phone and exchanged messages while preparing to meet in person as of 2025.How did a father’s search for his missing daughter lead him to MexicoAndrea Reyes was nearing her second birthday when she disappeared in 1999. Her mother, Rosa Tenorio, took her from a scheduled visitation in New Haven, Connecticut, and left for Mexico, according to police. Tenorio did not have custody rights, while Andrea’s father, Carlos Reyes-Couvertier, had legal custody of the child. After the disappearance, New Haven police worked with the FBI to try to find Andrea.City police obtained an arrest warrant for Tenorio on an alleged felony custodial interference charge. Authorities said the warrant remained valid, but only within the United States. The search eventually went cold despite police investigations and publicity around Andrea’s disappearance. However, Reyes-Couvertier continued looking for his daughter, making repeated trips to Mexico and following up on leads.A search in Mexico fails to reunite father with missing daughterThe search continued across borders, but authorities did not bring Andrea back to the United States. In the spring of 2000, officials in Puebla informed authorities in Connecticut that Andrea and her mother had been located in Mexico. However, New Haven police said no action was taken to bring the child back. Mexican officials said they did not consider parental kidnapping an offence covered by the extradition treaty between Mexico and the United States. Andrea remained in Mexico, while her father continued trying to find her.The case eventually went cold despite efforts by New Haven police, the FBI and the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children. Reyes-Couvertier also made multiple trips to Mexico in the hope of finding his daughter and reuniting with her.How a renewed investigation and DNA testing identified AndreaIn 2023, New Haven Detective Kealyn Nivakoff reopened the investigation as part of her work with the department's Special Victims Unit, which focuses on missing-person cases. Using search warrants, interviews and social media, she identified a woman living in Puebla whom she believed could be Andrea. Nivakoff then contacted her to investigate the possibility.Working with DNA testing company Othram, the detective arranged for Andrea to provide a DNA sample. Investigators compared it with a sample from Reyes-Couvertier. The results confirmed that the two were father and daughter, police said. After being decades apart, they were finally able to reconnect.Father describes joy of reconnecting with daughter after 25 yearsReyes-Couvertier and Andrea have spoken on the phone and exchanged messages since they reconnected. They were hoping to meet in person soon, but Andrea was still in Mexico and did not attend the March 12, 2025, news conference in New Haven.Reyes-Couvertier, then 55, described reconnecting with his daughter for the first time in more than 25 years as a moment of joy. He said, “We have some sense of happiness, but the chapter is not closed yet. There’s a lot of steps that we have to take.” The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children was helping prepare them for a reunion.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: New Delhi: Self-enumeration for the population enumeration phase of Census 2027 began on Monday in UP, Punjab, Goa and non-snow-bound areas of Uttarakhand. It will run till Nov 30, followed by house-to-house enumeration from Dec 1. The exercise will collect data across 40 fields, including caste. The question is open-ended and reply will be recorded as declared by the respondent. No documentary proof or verification is required.MHA's Sept 5 notification advanced the exercise in the four states ahead of assembly polls early next year. It will run till Jan 4, 2027, followed by a revisional round from Jan 5 to 9.Though Manipur is due for assembly polls, the census there has been postponed until further notice amid demands for a National Register of Citizens (NRC) exercise first. Houselisting operations, Phase I, are complete in all 35 states/UTs except Manipur.In remaining states/UTs, population enumeration will be held from Jan 25 to Feb 28, 2027, followed by a revisional round from Mar 1 to 5. Self-enumeration will be available from Jan 10 to 24. For the first time, Census 2027 is using digital tools. The web-based self-enumeration facility is available in 16 Indian languages. articles.body: NEW YORK: A gunman was found dead from a self-inflicted gunshot wound after shooting two public safety officers at a residential apartment complex in New York City's Bronx borough on Monday, police said. The two officers sustained injuries that were not believed to be life-threatening.The shooting took place at the massive Co-op City residential complex, where the suspected shooter barricaded himself inside an apartment following the attack. Police later found him dead inside the apartment.The New York Police Department (NYPD) confirmed that the two injured men were officers with the Co-op City Department of Public Safety, a private security force responsible for the residential complex. Both were taken to a hospital for treatment.Police initially reported that three people had been wounded but later revised the toll to two victims.The shooting unfolded inside one of the high-rise buildings at Co-op City, prompting authorities to evacuate the building as police officers and emergency personnel arrived at the scene.Mo Bee, who was working at a podiatry office in the building, said authorities announced the evacuation after arriving at the complex. He went outside and saw a large number of police officers and emergency vehicles across the residential campus.“It was “a pretty crazy scene,” said Bee, adding that he was allowed back in after about two hours. No patients were in the office at the time of the shooting.The complex's emergency dispatchers said they had no information about the incident, while its property management directed inquiries to the NYPD.Co-op City is a large residential complex in the Bronx, developed during the 1960s and 1970s to provide middle-income housing.The complex has more than 15,300 cooperative apartments spread across high-rise buildings and townhouses and is home to approximately 50,000 residents.The shooting prompted a police response and evacuation in the densely populated residential complex.You use AI every day. articles.title: First since 2015: No 'severe' AQI days for Delhi during November 1-15
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: What is usually Delhi's most polluted fortnight, from Nov 1 to 15, has ended this year without a single severe air quality day for the first
articles.body: NEW DELHI: What is usually Delhi's most polluted fortnight, from Nov 1 to 15, has ended this year without a single severe air quality day for the first time. A severe day means an AQI above 400 on a scale up to 500.Data from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), which began calculating the Air Quality Index (AQI) in April 2015, shows that Delhi recorded three severe days during this period in 2025, two in 2024, six in 2023, three in 2022, seven in 2021 and eight in 2020. The number of such days when AQI surpassed 400 was six in 2019, five in 2018, seven in 2017, nine in 2016 and three in 2015. The average AQI during this fortnight was 343 this year as compared to 367 last year and was the same as in 2022.Experts said better meteorological conditions, new stations recording lower readings, restrictions under the Graded Response Action Plan and Delhi's winter framework and low contribution of stubble burning likely prevented AQI from a further rise.On Diwali night, CPCB did not share the readings for several hours for many stations when the particulate matter concentrations surpassed 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre. This missing data was not considered for the calculation of the 24-hour average AQI.Sunil Dahiya, founder of think tank Envirocatalyst, said Delhi didn’t record severe air pollution this Nov because weather conditions were favourable. “While wind direction helped around Diwali, it was the most stagnant start to Nov on record. Less stubble smoke reached the city this year than in the heavy-burning years. Part of the no ‘severe’ day headline is also arithmetic; the bigger monitoring network, with newer lower-reading stations, pulled the city average down. On the long-running stations alone, Delhi crossed into ‘severe’ on three days,” said Dahiya.Another expert said, “Many stations have been recording severe air quality in Nov. However, new monitoring stations have seen lower AQI which have affected the city average.” He added, “On Diwali night, particulate matter concentrations at many stations surpassed 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre which was not considered for the 24-hour average AQI.”TOI reported that missing PM2.5 data could have pushed Delhi’s average pollution levels 49% higher on Diwali, according to an analysis by Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). Had the missing readings been recorded at 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre, the city’s average PM2.5 level would have increased from 269 to 400 micrograms per cubic metre, it revealed.Nov 1-15 is typically the capital’s most polluted period, with the average AQI at 374. In the first fortnight of Nov this year, Delhi recorded three poor days (AQI between 201 and 300) and 12 very poor days (AQI between 301 and 400). The highest AQI was recorded at 382 on Nov 6. However, the AQI remained in the severe category for a few hours on the morning of Nov 13, but the favourable weather factors brought down the 24-hour average AQI to 373.However, experts emphasised that the worst is not over yet. The city usually records severe air quality in Dec and Jan. The analysis of CPCB data showed that the second most polluted fortnight in a year is from Dec 16 to 31 with an average AQI of 346. This fortnight witnesses low temperatures and dense fog which traps pollutants. It also records increased traffic and use of firecrackers due to wedding season, Christmas and New Year’s Eve. Last year, this period saw five severe days, including a severe-plus day when AQI touched 461.The third most polluted spell is typically from Jan 1 to 15 when the unfavourable meteorological conditions, including dense fog, low temperatures and calm winds, continue. The average AQI of the period from Jan 1 to 15 was 329.3 during the period from 2016 to 2026.Meanwhile, Delhi’s AQI was 275 in the poor range Monday. Sirifort was the lone station to witness severe air quality at 441. The air quality of Delhi is forecast to worsen to very poor Tuesday.Biomass burning, including stubble burning, domestic solid biofuel, dung cakes and wood, was the dominant source of pollution, accounting for 30.9% in Delhi’s PM2.5 between 1 am and 9 am Monday. It was followed by mixed combustion at 27%, secondary organic aerosols at 19.6% and secondary inorganic aerosols at 8.8%, according to the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology’s real-time source apportionment data.
